FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (Part 1) (Fourth Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft 
finalized by the Statistical Methods for Quality and Reliability Sectional Committee had been approved by the 
Management and Systems Division Council. 


This standard 15 one of the series of Indian Standards on ‘Statistical test of significance’. Other standards published 
so far in the series are: 


Part 2 x? - test 
Part 3 Tests for normality 
Part 4 Non-parametric tests 


This standard was originally published in 1971 and covered the industrial applications of three main tests of 
significance, namely, t-test, F-test and y?-test. It was then revised in 1977 into four parts to include tests for 
normality as also some non-parametric tests, which have wide application in industry. It was further revised in 
1995 to rearrange the contents of the standard by putting together tests of the same hypothesis under different 
assumptions and requiring different use of test statistics. In addition, the revised standard includes: 


a) the basic concepts of formation of null and alternative hypothesis; 


b) Fisher-Behren's test for testing equality of means of two populations when the variances are not known 
and not assumed to be equal; and 


c) examples on testing for proportions. 
The third revision of the standard was undertaken to: 


a) modify the examples so as to make them practical and also that the reported test results to be of same 
decimal places as actually obtained in practice, 


b) include the table for finding 0 from tan 0 to be used in Fisher-Behren's test, and 
с) incorporate many editorial corrections. 


This revision has been taken up for technical modifications with regard to paired t-test and inclusion of more 
illustrative examples including those for formation of null hypothesis. 


The tests of significance described in this standard are useful in many problems of industrial experimentation. 


However, they should not be generally used for lot acceptance purposes for which IS 2500 (Part 1) : 2000 ‘Sampling 
inspection procedures: Part 1 Attribute sampling plans indexed by acceptable quality level (AQL) for lot-by-lot 
inspection’ and IS 2500 (Part 2): 1965 ‘Sampling inspection procedures: Part 2 Inspection by variables for percent 
defective’ may be referred to. 


IS 6200 (Part 1) : 2018 


Indian Standard 


STATISTICAL TESTS OF SIGNIFICANCE 
PART 1 NORMAL, t- AND F- TESTS 


(Fourth Revision) 


1 SCOPE 


1.1 This standard (Part 1) lays down the following tests 
of significance: 


а) One-sample test — Testing of mean of a 
population against a specified value: 
1) when the population variance 1s known, 
and 
2) when the population variance is not 
known. 
b) Two-samples test — Testing equality of means 
of two populations: 
1) when the variances are known, and 
2) when the variances are not known. 
c) Testing for equality of variances of two 
populations. 
d) Testing for proportions. 


1.2 This standard does not include Ше t-tests for 
regression coefficient and correlation coefficient as they 
are covered in IS 7300 ‘Methods of regression and 
correlation'.

through reference in this text constitute provisions of 
this standard. At the time of publication, the editions 
indicated were valid. All standards are subject to 
revision and parties to agreements based on this 
standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility 
of applying the most recent editions of the standards

3 TERMINOLOGY 


For the purpose of this standard, the definitions given 
in IS 7920 (Part 1) and IS 7920 (Part 2) shall apply. 


4 BASIC CONCEPTS 


4.1 Statistical tests of significance are important tools in 


decision-making. They are extremely useful in finding 
out whether, in the case of one population, the mean 
value differs significantly from certain specified value 
or whether, in the case of two populations, the mean 
values differ significantly from each other. Thus, it may 
be desirable to find out whether a new germicide is more 
effective in treating a certain type of infection than a 
standard germicide, whether a new method of sealing 
light bulbs will increase their life or whether one method 
of preserving foods 15 better than another in so far as the 
retention of vitamins is concerned. In such cases, it would 
be necessary to examine whether the mean values 
obtained can be deemed as same or different. There may 
also be cases where it may be worthwhile to find out 
whether one inspector is more consistent than another 
or whether a new source of raw material has resulted in 
a change in the variability of the output or whether the 
temperature of the bath in which the cocoons are cooked 
affects the uniformity of the quality of silk. In these cases 
it will be necessary to determine whether the variances 
obtained are the same or not. 


4.2 Formulation of Hypothesis 


For taking a decision whether a statement about the 
value of a population parameter should or should not 
be rejected using statistical tests of significance, the 
first step is to form the hypotheses, namely, Null 
hypothesis (Н) and Alternative hypothesis (И). The 
two hypotheses are tested using the data from a sample. 


4.2.1 Null Hypothesis (Но) 


The procedure commonly used is to first make a tentative 
assumption about a population parameter called the null 
hypothesis regarding equivalence (no difference). The 
question, on which the decision is called for, by applying 
the tests of significance, is translated in terms of null 
hypothesis in such a way that this null hypothesis would 
likely be rejected if there is enough evidence against it 
as seen from the data in the sample. For example, in the 
case of new germicide, a null hypothesis will be that it is 
not more effective than a standard germicide; or in the 
case of light bulbs the new method of sealing does not 
increase the life of the bulb. 


4.2.2 Alternative Hypothesis (Hj) 


Alternative hypothesis 1s opposite to what 15 stated in 
the null hypothesis. It may be two-sided or one-sided. 


IS 6200 (Part 1) : 2018 


4.2.2.1 Two-sided hypothesis 


In some situations, it may be of interest to find out 
whether lot mean differs significantly from a specified 
value irrespective of the fact that this difference is 
positive or negative. For example, in the manufacture of 
certain cylindrical rods, one may have to examine 
whether average diameter differs significantly from the 
specified nominal value or one may wish to determine 
whether the night shift production differs from that of 
the day shift in respect of certain quality characteristics 
of the item. In such cases the test is said to be two-sided. 


Example 1 


A multispindle filling machine operation is designed 
to fill HDPE woven bags with Ordinary Portland 
Cement (OPC), 33 grade to a mean weight of 10 kg. A 
sample of bags is periodically taken for weighment. If 
the sample data leads to a conclusion of underfilling or 
overfilling, the production line will be stopped and 
adjusted to ensure proper filling. 


In this case, the null and alternative hypothesis would 
be formulated as follows: 

Ay: uw = 10 

H,:u*10 
If the sample results indicate that H, cannot be rejected, 
the bags will be accepted. However, if the sample results 
indicate that Н be rejected, the decision will be taken 
that the bags do not meet the weight specification. In 
this case, there 15 sufficient evidence to stop the 
machine. 


4.2.2.2 One-sided hypothesis 


In some other situations, only the positive difference 
or the negative difference between the lot mean and 
specified value may be of interest. For example, when 
drinking water is tested for bacteria count, only high 
values of count may be the source of concern or when 
cases of concrete are tested for strength, low values 
may have to be detected. In such cases, the test 1s said 
to be one-sided. 


Example 2 


Consider a situation of a manufacturer of gold plated 
watches who states that thickness of gold plating on 
watches is 3 microns at the minimum. A sample of gold 
plated watches will be drawn and the thickness of gold 
will be measured for testing the validity of the 
manufacturer's claims. 


In such situations we generally assume that the 
manufacture's claim is true and the null hypothesis and 
the alternate hypothesis will be stated as follows: 


Ay: uw 2 3 
Н:и<3 


If the sample results indicate H, not be rejected, Ше 
manufacturer’s claim will not be challenged. However, 
if the sample results indicate that H, can be rejected, 
the decision will be that H, : и < 3 is true, that is, 
statistical evidence indicates that the manufacturer’s 
claim is incorrect and the mean gold plating in watches 
is less than the claimed 3 microns. 


4.3 Type I and Type П Errors 


4.3.1 There are two kinds of errors involved in taking 
the decision based on the tests of significance, namely: 


a) Type I error — Error in deciding that a 
significant difference exists when there is no 
real difference, that is, H, is rejected when it 
is true. 

b) Type П error — Error in deciding that no 
difference exists when there is a real 
difference, that is, H, is accepted when it is 
not true. 

4.3.2 Type I error and Type П error are also called error 
of the first kind and error of the second kind 
respectively. This process of decision-making is given 
below: 


Decision Н, True На True 
Reject Ho Туре I error (a) Correct decision 
Accept Ho Correct decision Type II error (В) 


4.4 Level of Significance 


Based on the distribution of test statistics used, it is 
possible to work out the probability of committing Type 
I error or Type II error. The probability of committing 
Type I error, when the null hypothesis is true is called 
level of significance (о). It is not possible to minimize 
both these probabilities (risk) at the same time. Hence, 
one of the risks, usually of the first kind, 1s controlled 
by assigning it a chosen level of probability. Generally 
the value for level of significance 15 chosen as 0.05 or 
0.01, that is, 5 percent or 1 percent. This implies 
confidence level of 95 percent or 99 percent 
respectively. 


4.5 The decision-making procedure involves the 
comparison of the calculated value of the test statistic 
with the tabulated value. If the calculated value is 
greater than or equal to the tabulated value of the 
statistic, then Н is rejected, thereby accepting Hj; 
otherwise తో 15 not rejected. For practical purpose, ‘Ho 
is not rejected’ is taken as “తో is accepted’. 


If the value is smaller than the tabulated value 
at 5 percent level of significance, the difference is given 
benefit of doubt due to sampling error and is considered 
not significant. If it is greater than the tabulated value 


at 5 percent level of significance and less than 1 percent 
level of significance then it is considered as significant. 
If it exceeds tabulated value of 1 percent, the difference 
is considered highly significant. 


4.6 p-value Approach 


In statistical tests of significance, p-value is the 
probability of obtaining a result equal to or more 
extreme than what was actually observed, assuming that 
the null hypothesis is true. The p-value is used to 
determine whether the null hypothesis should be 
rejected. Smaller is the p-value, larger the significance. 
Null hypothesis is rejected when the p-value is less than 
a predetermined level of significance, 0.05 or 0.01, that 
is, at 5 percent or 1 percent, otherwise Н, is accepted. 


4.7 For each test of significance, certain underlying 
assumptions are made (see 5.1 and 8.2). Hence, it 1s 
important that these tests are not used indiscriminately. 
If the assumptions are in doubt, it is advisable to obtain 
the guidance of a competent statistician to ascertain 
the feasibility of application of appropriate tests. 


5 ONE SAMPLE TEST — TESTING OF MEAN 
OF A POPULATION AGAINST A SPECIFIED 
VALUE 


5.1 To judge whether the population mean (и) differs 
significantly from a specified value, и, a sample of

1s calculated. 


In this case, null hypothesis is: Н: и = и 


Depending upon the situation, any one of the following 
three alternative hypotheses may be selected: 


a) H,:u* u,(two-sided), 

b) H,:u 7 u,(one-sided), and 

c) H,:u  u,(one-sided). 
It is assumed that the observations follow normal 
distribution and are drawn at random. Depending upon 
the knowledge about the population variance, two cases 
may arise as given below. 


5.2 Population Variance (o?) is Known 


In this case the normal (z) test is applied by computing 
the statistic

A sample of size 10 from a consignment of resistors

The t-test is used for small samples (n < 30). When

5.3.2 Example 2 


The measurement of the diameters (in mm) of 15 pins 
manufactured by a machine gives the values as: 


19.5 22.4 19.7 18.8 19.8 20.1 223 20.3 
21.8 20.9 21.7 16.9 184 18.5 21.7 


It is required to find out whether the average diameter 
of the pins differs significantly from the specified 
diameter of 20.0 mm or not. 


Solution 


The mean (x ) and the standard deviation (s) of the 
sample measurements are found to be 20.19 and 
1.62 mm respectively. 


The null hypothesis is that the mean diameter of the 
pins manufactured by this machine is equal to 20.0 mm, 
that is, Но: u = 20.0. 

The alternative hypothesis is two-sided, given as, 
A: u # 20.0. 


The t-test is applied by calculating: 
t=| x-uy|Nn/s. = [20.19-20.00 | 15/1.62 =0.454 


Since the calculated value of # is less than 2.145, the 
tabulated value of t at 5 percent level of significance 
(two-sided) with 14 degrees of freedom (see Annex B), 
the validity of the null hypothesis 15 not rejected at 
5 percent level of significance and the population mean 
diameter is taken to be in agreement with the specified 
diameter of 20.0 mm.

statistic f 


p-value corresponding to test statistic t — 0.454 with

0.05, the level of significance, а. Therefore the null 
hypothesis is not rejected. 


NOTE—p-values can be obtained using any statistical software. 
5.3.3 Example 3 


A manufacturer produces a special alloy steel with an 
average tensile strength of 180.0 MPa. A change in the 
composition of the alloy is said to increase the tensile 
strength without affecting the variability. Ten tests done 
on the steel with the new composition gave the 
following values (in MPa): 


178.2 180.5 181.8 182.4 182.8 183.1 183.4 183.8 
183.9 185.6 


It is required to find out whether the average tensile 
strength is significantly more than 180.0 MPa obtained 
for the earlier composition. 


Solution 


The mean (x ) and the standard deviation (5) of the 
sample test results are obtained as 182.55 and 2.04 
respectively. 


The null hypothesis (А) is that the mean tensile strength 
for the new composition is same as that for the earlier 
composition (equal to 180 MPa), against the alternative 
hypothesis that the new composition gives higher tensile 
strength than 180 MPa. 


The t-test is applied by calculating: 
t = (182.55 — 180.0) V10 / 2.04 = 3.95 


Since the calculated value of ¢ is greater than 1.833 
and 2.821, the tabulated values at 5 percent and 
1 percent levels of significance respectively, with 9 
degrees of freedom for one-sided test (see Annex B), 
the null hypothesis is rejected at 5 percent level of 
significance and it is concluded that the mean tensile 
strength of the steel with new composition is 
significantly higher than 180.0 M Pa corresponding to 
the earlier composition. 


5.3.3.1 Using p-value 


p-value = Probability of obtaining a value for the test 
statistic f 


p- value corresponding to test statistic t — 3.95 with 9 
degrees of freedom is 0.001 677 which is less than level 
of significance 0.05 and 0.01. The null hypothesis is 
rejected (not accepted) at 5 percent as well as 1 percent 
level of significance.

6.3 Population Variances are not Known

satisfied. The pooled variance s” has, in fact, been

The rules for rejection of the null hypothesis regarding

6.3.2 Independent Populations with Variances not 
Assumed to be Equal 


In this case, Fisher-Behren's test is applied by 
computing the following statistic: 


d-|x-»l/tis2/Q -1) + (s2/(- 1)}]°

6.3.3 Related Populations (Paired t-Test) 


In some situations, the difference between two 
dependent observations is of more interest than the 
individual observations. Thus the observations may 
occur in pairs, each pair arising under the same 
experimental conditions with the conditions varying 
from pair to pair. In such a case the differences between 
the observations in each pair are taken and t-test 15 
applied on these differences. The null hypothesis is that 
the mean ofthe differences is zero against the alternative 
hypothesis that the mean of the difference is not equal 
to zero. 


6.3.3.1 Example 6 


The test results for compressive strength of 16 cements 
using two grades of standard sand are obtained as in 
col 2 and 3 of Table 3. It is required to examine whether 
or not there is a significant effect of the grade of sand 
on the average compressive strength of cements. 


Solution 


Xd =-1.2 and Ха? = 0.48

6.3.3.3 If the number of observations in the sample, n, 
becomes large, the t-test becomes equivalent to the 
Normal test. When the sample size is greater than 30, 
Normal test may be used instead of t-test for all practical 
purposes. 


7 TESTING FOR PROPORTION 


7.1 The normal test described in 5.2 and 6.2 may also 
be extended to the testing for proportions. If the 
binomial proportion p (obtained as the ratio of the 
number of successes in п repetitive trials) is to be tested 
against a specified value p, then the null hypothesis 15 
Hy: p = Po against the three possible alternative 
hypotheses, namely 


H: те p, (two-sided) 
H: т € p, (one-sided) 
H: T> p, (one-sided) 
where л is the population proportion of success. Further,

the z-statistic to be calculated 1s obtained as 


z-|P - poll [po (1 – ро) / п]? for H: tZ pg

The tabulated values of z are given in Annex A. These 
values will be used in taking the decision as per 4.4. 


7.1.1 Example 8 


A purchaser picks up at random a sample of size 15 
from a lot and finds one non-conforming item. It is 
required to test the hypothesis that the lot contains 5 
percent non-conforming items. 


Here, p = 1/15 = 0.067; n 5/100 — 0.05 


15; po 


To examine if the proportion non-conforming in the 
lot, ро 15 0.05, the null hypothesis Ну: т = ро is tested 
against the alternative hypothesis И: л = ро 


The z statistic is calculated as 
=| 0.067 – 0.05|/ [0.05(1 — 0.05) /15]* 
= 0.017 / 0.056 = 0.30 


This value is less than 1.96, the tabulated value of z at 5 
percent level of significance (two-sided) (see Annex A). 
Hence, the null hypothesis that the proportion non- 
conforming in the lot is 0.05 is not rejected. 


7.2 In the case of testing the equality of two proportions 
corresponding to two populations, if p, and p, are the 
two proportions obtained on the basis of samples of 
size n, and n, drawn from the two populations 
respectively, then calculate: 


р'= (тру + пор») / (n + nj) 


In this case, the null hypothesis is Hp: п, = л, against 
the alternative hypothesis Н, : ли + m, or H,: n < m, or

for Н : T< m; 
The rules for rejecting or not rejecting the null

7.2.1 Example 9 


A machine puts out 20 imperfect articles in a sample of 
500. After machine is overhauled, it produced 3 
imperfect articles in a batch of 100. Has the machine 
improved? 


Here, n, = 500, p, = 20/500 = 0.04, п, = 100, 
p 473/100 = 0.03 


The null hypothesis is Ну: т, = л, and the alternative 
hypothesis 15 И, : 1, >л, 


р' = ( 500 x 0.04 + 100 x 0.03) / (500 + 100) = 0.038 


The test statistic 15 computed as: 


z-(Ppi-P3/[p' (1-р') (n + nj)/ тп]? 
=(0.04 — 0.03) / [ 0.038 (1 — 0.038) (500 + 100) / 
500 x 100]^ 
=0.01/0.021 = 0.48 
This value is less than 1.645, the tabulated value of z at 
5 percent level of significance (one-sided) (see 


Annex A). Hence the null hypothesis is not rejected, 
that is the machine has not improved. 


8 TESTING EQUALITY OF VARIANCES 


8.1 To test the equality of the variances of the two 
populations, say 6,2 and o,”, null hypothesis is, 
Ну: сү 0,7. 
The alternative hypothesis may be one-sided or two- 
sided as: 

Н;: о 0, (two-sided), and 

H, : o> с,2 (one-sided). 
Thus, if the variances of the samples of sizes n, and n, 


from the two populations be з 2 and 5,2, respectively, 
the following statistic is computed: 


F= s,?/ 5,2 for Ну: сү” # 0 
F-s sy for Ну: с> с) 
Е = 512/5 ,2 for Ну: с2< 605

The larger of two variances is taken in the numerator. 
The value of F is associated with (n,—1), (1-1) degrees 
of freedom when 5,2“ 5,2. In case 5,2 is greater than 51“, 
the degrees of freedom would be ( n, — 1), (n, - 1). 


The tabulated values of F are given in Annex E. These 
values will be used for taking the decision as per 4.4. 


8.1.1 Example 10 


There are two alternative methods X and Y available

ona given sample and 15 determinations by Method Y

results. 


Solution 


The variances of the two sets of results as indicated in 
8.1 are obtained as 


512 =0.062 for Method X, and

Bureau of Indian Standards 

BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote 
harmonious development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods 
and attending to connected matters in the country. 

Copyright 

BIS has the copyright of all its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced in any form 
without the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course of 
implementing the standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. 
Enquiries relating to copyright be addressed to the Director (Publications), BIS. 

Review of Indian Standards 

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of 


‘BIS Catalogue’ and ‘Standards : Monthly Additions’. 


This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc No.: MSD 03 (0477).
